job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Umar Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for your time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in robotics and embedded systems at Calder University, and my days are split between lectures, the robotics lab and a garage where my friend Sami and I are building a small crop-monitoring drone. I live in student housing, but my parents' grocery shop, Haddad Fresh, is a bus ride away and I'm there on Sundays. I have no debt, because my uncle's help and my own savings covered the bachelor's.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does AI do in your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Everything small. It drafts the boring parts of my code, explains datasheets, and summarises papers while I eat breakfast. My bachelor's in electronic engineering was just a pass, since I spent exam season on the drone, so I like that the tools let me move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, and I'd keep using what works. I'd tell my lab mates the hype always overshoots, so we should build for real customers. Online I'd post a short video of the drone and say nothing about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the plan is easy. Finish the master's, then work at an embedded company for two or three years, while the drone side project grows. I have over six months saved and Calder has plenty of electronics employers. A plateau actually helps small makers like us, because the market stays predictable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to about ten embedded firms for next summer, and keep building the drone on weekends. I'd put a small part of my savings into a basic index fund, around two thousand, and leave the rest. I'd also pitch the drone to two farms near Calder for a test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit impatient. I'd like things to move faster than they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a slower AI world change the drone project?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It wouldn't change it. The drone needs a camera, a flight controller and farmers who trust us, none of which is an AI thing. If AI helped a bit, it saves me a day per week on code, and I spend that on the field tests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you decide when to invest your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep it simple. A basic index fund for the long term and a drone fund for parts. I don't buy anything I can't explain to my dad in a minute, because he'd ask me twice.

say: I'd say fine, and keep using what works: the hype always **overshoots**.
I'd post a short **drone video** and say nothing about AI.
think: The plan is easy: finish the master's, then work at an **embedded firm** for two or three years.
A plateau helps small makers, because the market stays **predictable**.
do: Apply to about ten **embedded firms** and keep building the drone on weekends.
Put two thousand into a basic **index fund** and pitch two farms.
feel: **Calm** and a bit impatient, since I'd like things to move faster.
S0.quote: I don't buy anything I can't explain to my dad in a minute, because he'd ask me twice.
fieldNote: A **maker's calm**: a predictable market suits the side project and the day job together.
Handles his savings with a **simple rule**, which shows adaptive but not reckless risk-taking.

steps.text: Apply to ten embedded firms for next summer
Pitch the crop-monitoring drone to two farms for a field test
Put two thousand into a basic index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when small teams win, since one person with good tools can do what ten did. I'd tell friends to learn the tools and use them on something real. Online I'd share what I've built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm well placed. Entry-level coding jobs will thin out, but I'm learning embedded and robotics, where software meets real hardware. My pass degree is a weakness on paper, but I have a drone that flies. I think a lot of graduates with better grades and no projects are in more trouble than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and start a company with Sami around the drone, selling crop monitoring to farms as a service. I'd also take a part-time embedded job to pay the bills. I'd put aside three months' pay as a buffer and invest the rest of my savings gradually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a slight guilt that some friends can't do this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your first-year plan look like if the tools got stronger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami and I would lean on the tools for coding, mapping and the reports, and spend our human time with the farmers. If a farmer wants to know why a field has a yellow patch, the tool shows the picture and I have to climb out and look at the soil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your parents' shop staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad's shop staff, mostly three part-timers, to use whatever software handles stock ordering, since it saves them hours. My cousin Nada does the shop's ordering and I'd set up a simple tool for her one afternoon.

say: This is when **small teams win**: one person with good tools does what ten did.
I'd tell friends to use the tools on something **real**.
think: Entry coding jobs thin out, but **embedded and robotics** put software in contact with hardware.
I have a **drone that flies**, which beats better grades with no projects.
do: Start a company with Sami selling **crop monitoring** to farms as a service.
Take a part-time **embedded job** and keep three months' pay as a buffer.
feel: **Excited**, with a little guilt that some friends can't do this.
S1.quote: I have a drone that flies. I think a lot of graduates with better grades and no projects are in more trouble than me.
fieldNote: His adaptability makes the world look like a **chance**, while he admits his pass degree is weak on paper.
Brings in a **cousin's shop ordering** as a concrete example of helping others use the tools.

steps.text: Start a crop-monitoring company with Sami around the drone
Take a part-time embedded engineering job for income
Set up a stock ordering tool for cousin Nada at the shop
Keep three months of pay as a buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest change in our lifetimes and people should be honest about it. At the lab I'd say we have a short window to get something real built. Online I'd share facts and not hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy rather than scared. My own work, embedded and drones, depends on hardware, and robots reach hands-on work around 2031, which gives me three years after the thinking part is done. But my parents' shop and my uncle's accounting job would be in trouble sooner, and that bothers me more than my own situation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speed everything up. Sami and I would launch the drone service by summer, sell it to as many farms as we can, and use AI for design and testing. I'd keep my savings liquid, apart from a little in the index fund, and tell my parents to avoid new loans for the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with energy. I'd be working harder than ever, and I'd also be worried about the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you even though you're well placed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' shop sells food, which people still need. But the supply chains, the pricing, the ordering would all be handled by systems, and bigger chains would crush a small shop. My father would hear that as a bad prediction, and he wouldn't be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your father that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Baba, I'm not going to tell you what to do with the shop, but I'd like to make a plan with you for three scenarios. He'd laugh and tell me to eat first. Then he'd listen, because he always does.

say: It's the **biggest change** in our lifetimes, and people should be honest about it.
At the lab I'd say we have a **short window**.
think: My own work depends on **hardware**, which gives me about three years after the thinking part is done.
My parents' shop and my uncle's **accounting job** worry me more than I do.
do: Launch the **drone service** by summer and sell it to as many farms as possible.
Keep savings **liquid** and tell my parents to avoid new shop loans.
feel: Uneasy, with **energy**, working harder and worrying about family.
S2.quote: I'm not going to tell you what to do with the shop, but I'd like to make a plan with you for three scenarios.
fieldNote: He is uneasy for **others**, not himself: his own field is hardware-heavy and buys him time.
Speaks to his father with **respect**, offering a plan, and Baba is his word for father.

steps.text: Launch the drone service by summer and sign several farms
Use AI tools for drone design and field testing
Keep savings liquid apart from the index fund
Make a three-scenario plan with my father for the shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build something and short enough to hurry. I'd tell friends to start companies, or at least learn a lot of skills. Online I'd talk about building, not worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm pretty calm. I'd have three or four years of work and the drone company growing before the thinking AI arrives, and my hardware knowledge helps for another three years after that. I'd have savings, contacts and options, which is what I want to have in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take an embedded job, and push the drone company on the side until it can pay me. I'd put about a third of my pay into an index fund and some into the drone. I'd also learn the newest tools every few months and write down what changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit eager. It's the sort of thing that makes me want to build faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having five years change your approach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a lot. With five years I can let the company grow in stages: first the drone, then a software layer, then perhaps robots for the farm work itself. In two years I'd have to skip stages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want on your team in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami for hardware, my friend Elif for sales, since she can talk to farmers, and maybe my cousin Nada for the books. I'd want people who are good at things I'm bad at, and who like fieldwork.

say: Five years is **long enough** to build something and short enough to hurry.
I'd tell friends to start companies or learn **many skills**.
think: I'd have three or four years of work and a **growing drone company** before thinking AI arrives.
My hardware knowledge helps for another three years, so I'd have **options** by 2031.
do: Take an embedded job and push the **drone company** until it can pay me.
Put a third of my pay into an **index fund** and some into the drone.
feel: Calm and **eager**: it makes me want to build faster.
S3.quote: I'd want people who are good at things I'm bad at, and who like fieldwork.
fieldNote: Time lets him build in **stages**, from drone to software to farm robots, and he knows it.
Names a **team** with real roles, showing he thinks like a founder rather than an employee.

steps.text: Take an embedded engineering job and keep the drone company running
Put a third of my pay into an index fund
Test the newest AI tools every few months and note changes
Hire Elif for sales and Nada for the books

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone who uses it. I'd tell friends to start experimenting now and not wait for permission. Online I'd talk about tools and training and keep it hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm. By 2036 I'd be thirty-four, with a company or a senior job, maybe both, and a decade of tool experience. Robots arrive around 2039, and I'd likely be building the farm side of that, not competing with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work at an embedded firm for two years, then take the drone company full-time. I'd invest steadily and buy a small flat in Calder. I'd use each new tool as it arrives, since I'm already doing that and enjoying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. I like when the future is far enough to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first, and what would you leave for later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First the job and the savings, so I can afford to take a risk. Later the company, the property and maybe a second business. I'd leave anything that needs a big hire until I'm sure of the customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to people who feel stuck?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say stuck isn't a permanent state. Pick one small thing, like a tool, a course or a project, and do it for a month. I've watched my friend Karim go from never touching these tools to building his own, in about six weeks.

say: Ten years is a **gift** for anyone who uses it.
I'd tell friends to experiment now and not wait for **permission**.
think: By 2036 I'd have a company or a **senior job**, maybe both.
I'd likely be building the **farm robot** side, not competing with it.
do: Work two years at an embedded firm, then take the **drone company** full-time.
Invest steadily and buy a small **flat** in Calder.
feel: Calm and **curious**: the future is far enough to plan.
S4.quote: Stuck isn't a permanent state. Pick one small thing, like a tool, a course or a project, and do it for a month.
fieldNote: His long horizon is full of **sequence**: job and savings first, company second, risk later.
Advice to others is concrete: **one small thing** for a month, backed by an example.

steps.text: Work two years at an embedded firm to save money
Take the drone company full-time after the savings are built
Buy a small flat in Calder
Learn each new AI tool as soon as it arrives

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, though mostly for my parents. My own plan survives it better than most, but their shop could be squeezed before they can change anything. What would help is cheap, simple tools for small shops and a bit of public support for their loans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just say that being good with the tools isn't something to be smug about. I see friends who aren't, and I'd rather help them than win.

headlineQuote: Being good with the tools isn't something to be smug about. I see friends who aren't, and I'd rather help them than win.
portrait: Umar is a **24-year-old** robotics master's student with a pass degree, no debt and a drone he and Sami built.
He uses AI **every day**, adapts fast and invests with a simple rule he could explain to his father.
He is centre-minded and sees change as a chance, with a **builder's** appetite for risk.
His mood is calm in most worlds and **uneasy** only when AGI arrives in two years.
Most of his unease is for his **parents' shop**, not for his own work.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, mostly for his parents' shop, which could be squeezed before it can change.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, simple tools for small shops and some **public support** for their loans.
